summary: This RFC describes using OSPFv3 as the routing protocol between Provider Edge and Customer Edge routers in BGP/MPLS VPNs. It is the IPv6 counterpart of the OSPFv2 arrangement.

eli5.summary: A company links to its provider through a gate router. This explains how they share route info using OSPFv3 over that link.

questions: what is a sham link in ospf
what is the dn-bit in ospf
subtitle: How IPv6 customer sites can run OSPFv3 to their provider and still see each other as one OSPF network across a BGP/MPLS VPN.

tldr.problem: BGP/MPLS VPNs already let customer routers exchange routes with the provider using OSPFv2, but only OSPFv2 was specified as the PE-CE protocol, so IPv6 customers using OSPFv3 had no standard to follow.
tldr.mechanism: OSPFv3 follows the same model as OSPFv2 PE-CE, with changes for OSPFv3: several instances per interface, new LSA types, extended communities that carry OSPF details across BGP, the DN-bit for loop prevention and 128-bit sham link endpoints.
tldr.outcome: A CE needs no VPN awareness and can run any OSPFv3 implementation. The PE-CE functionality is identical to OSPFv2 except for the differences this RFC lists.

today: RFC 6565 is a Proposed Standard (Standards Track) published in June 2012, and the unit metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why OSPFv3 Needs Its Own PE-CE Rules
sections.content:
RFC 4364 lets service providers offer Layer 3 VPNs. Provider Edge (PE) routers keep each customer's routes in a separate VRF table, and BGP carries those routes between PEs. The PE learns routes from the customer side by static routing or by a routing protocol running on the PE-CE link, and the original specification included BGP, RIP and OSPFv2 for that. RFC 4577 then detailed OSPFv2 as the PE-CE protocol.

RFC 4659 extended VPNs to IPv6. RFC 6565 expects that OSPFv3 will be used as the IGP for some IPv6 VPNs, just as OSPFv2 was for IPv4, and defines the mechanisms for it. It reuses and extends methods from RFC 4659 and RFC 4577, and readers are expected to know them along with RFC 5340 (OSPFv3) and RFC 2328.
sections.eli5: There was already a rule book for offices using the older address type. This one adds the matching rule book for the newer address type.

sections.title: VRFs, Instances and Domain IDs
sections.content:
The requirements in Section 3 of RFC 4577 stay semantically the same. What changes comes from OSPFv3 itself: it runs per link rather than per IP subnet, so multiple OSPFv3 instances can run over one interface. That changes the RFC 4577 rule of one OSPF instance per interface. A PE interface can be associated with only one VRF, and all instances on that interface MUST use the same VRF. Each instance is tied to a single VRF, and instances sharing a VRF do not leak routes to each other unless configured to.

Each OSPFv3 instance MUST have a primary Domain ID, which travels with the VPN-IPv6 route in a BGP attribute. It may also have secondary Domain IDs, but only if a non-NULL primary is configured. An incoming route is in the same domain if a non-NULL incoming Domain ID matches the local primary or a secondary one, or if both are NULL.

From the CE's point of view the PE looks like any other OSPFv3 neighbour, so the CE needs no awareness of the VPN. Each CE should see its connected PE as a separate router, since the VPN backbone cannot be treated as one router.
sections.eli5: The gate router looks like any other neighbour to the office. Each office can have several separate road-map clubs on the same cable, and each club belongs to just one company's network.

sections.title: Moving Routes Between OSPFv3 and BGP
sections.content:
A route learned by OSPFv3 on a PE gets an 8-octet Route Distinguisher, which turns the IPv6 prefix into a VPN-IPv6 prefix. It is then redistributed into MP-BGP with a Route Target extended community. A remote PE imports the route only if one of its VRFs has an identical import Route Target. The Route Distinguisher is removed before the IPv6 route is installed in the VRF. The BGP Multi-Exit-Discriminator SHOULD be set to the OSPFv3 metric plus 1.

When a PE passes a BGP-learned route to a CE, the type of LSA depends on where the route came from.

  • Inter-area: an Inter-Area-Prefix LSA (0x2003) when the route comes from the same OSPFv3 domain and was advertised to the remote PE in an Intra-Area-Prefix (0x2009) or Inter-Area-Prefix LSA. The PE then acts as an Area Border Router.
  • Intra-area: an Intra-Area-Prefix LSA (0x2009) only when sham links are used.
  • External: an AS-External LSA (0x4005), or an NSSA-LSA (0x2007) if the PE-CE link is in an NSSA, when the domain differs, when the route was external in the source domain, or when it was not learned from OSPFv3.

External routes get a Type-2 metric by default, unless the VPN-IPv6 route indicates Type-1 or local policy says otherwise. Whether a route is passed to a CE at all depends on local configuration and filtering.
sections.eli5: When a road map comes in from far away, the gate router decides how to label it for the local office: as a street in your own town, or as a road from another country.

sections.title: BGP Extended Communities for OSPFv3
sections.content:
OSPFv3-specific information has to cross the BGP backbone so the remote PE can rebuild a faithful picture. RFC 6565 reuses the extended communities from RFC 4577, and every OSPFv3 route in the VRF MUST carry the matching attributes.

  • OSPF Domain Identifier: a 6-byte Domain ID with a 2-byte type of 0x0005, 0x0105 or 0x0205. Its default value is 0.
  • OSPF Router ID: a 4-byte (32-bit) Router ID with type 0x0107. Setting it is OPTIONAL and the default is 0.
  • OSPF Route Type: MUST be present, with type 0x0306. It holds a 4-byte Area Number, a 1-byte Route Type and a 1-byte Options field.

The route type codes follow the OSPFv3 LSA types. In the Options byte, the least significant bit says whether the external metric is Type-1 (bit clear) or Type-2 (bit set).
sections.eli5: The road maps get little stickers saying which neighbourhood they came from, which router wrote them and what kind of road they are, so the far-away office can redraw them correctly.

sections.title: Loop Prevention with the DN-bit
sections.content:
Loops can happen, for example when a CE is dual-homed to two PEs. Those PEs hear routes both from the CE and from each other. The scenarios are the same as for OSPFv2 in RFC 4577. Of the two loop-prevention mechanisms there, only the DN-bit is supported for OSPFv3.

The DN-bit MUST be set in Inter-Area-Prefix, NSSA and AS-External LSAs when a PE originates them toward a CE. This stops those prefixes from being advertised back into BGP. An LSA with the DN-bit set must not be used for route calculations on PE routers. The DN-bit MUST be clear in all other LSA types. Caution is still needed if mutual redistribution on a PE loses the loop-prevention information.
sections.eli5: The DN-bit is a stamp saying this route came from the provider. The gate router will not send anything with that stamp back to the provider, so the maps cannot go round in circles.

sections.title: OSPFv3 Sham Links
sections.content:
A sham link lets the VPN backbone act as an intra-area link. It is needed when two sites also have an intra-area backdoor link and the inter-area backbone route would be less preferable under OSPF route preference rules. Support for OSPFv3 sham links is an OPTIONAL feature.

OSPFv3 sham links are identified by 128-bit endpoint addresses. These can no longer default to the 32-bit Router ID, so the endpoint addresses MUST be configured. They MUST be distributed by BGP as routable VPN-IPv6 addresses with a 128-bit prefix, and MUST NOT be advertised by OSPFv3. The sham link appears up only if there is a BGP route to the remote endpoint address.

Multiple OSPFv3 instances can run across one sham link, which still counts as a relation between two VRFs. The Instance ID in the packet header separates their packets. Sham links are treated as on-demand circuits. A route whose next-hop interface is a sham link SHOULD NOT be redistributed into BGP, and packets whose preferred route uses the sham link MUST be forwarded according to the corresponding BGP route.
sections.eli5: A sham link is a pretend road through the provider that the offices treat like a short private road, so traffic prefers it over a slow back alley between the offices.

sections.title: Multiple Address Families
sections.content: RFC 5838 supports several address families in OSPFv3 by reserving ranges of Instance IDs for each one. The architecture here is fully compatible with RFC 5838, so the OSPFv3 PE-CE protocol can support multiple address families across a VPN backbone. Every address family redistributed from OSPFv3 into BGP on a PE MUST carry the extended community attributes described above.
sections.eli5: The same system can carry maps for more than one kind of address, as long as each map gets its stickers.

sections.title: Security and IANA
sections.content:
The extensions are specific to OSPFv3 as the PE-CE protocol. They do not introduce new security concerns beyond those in Section 6 of RFC 4577.

An early version of this document led to an allocation of an OSPFv3 Route Attributes (0x0004) entry in the BGP IPv6 Address Specific Extended Community registry. That allocation is no longer required, and IANA has marked it deprecated. The extended communities used here were already registered.
sections.eli5: Nothing new is risky here beyond what the older rule book already warns about.
